summary:
The project was developed as an interactive map that designs fast and safe routes for the 3 key points along the Curiosity rover's trajectory. In the event of any emergency, the map features a built-in safety AI connected to satellites, rovers, and drones around Mars. Once these detect any hazard along the original routes, they send a signal to the AI so it can proceed to reroute the path, while also checking whether the crew's oxygen supply is sufficient for the desired trajectory, as well as logging each hazard and its coordinates in a flight log.

This map addresses this challenge effectively, fulfilling and improving upon the given requirements. It is vitally important because, thanks to it, astronauts can stay safe and reach their mission objectives securely while receiving guidance on routes and missions.
details:
Project Details: ARES Surface Explorer (MECAESTRELLAS)

1. What does it do and how does it work?

ARES Surface Explorer ("Following the Traces of Water") is an interactive planning, simulation, and tactical assistance map for human Extravehicular Activities (EVA) on the surface of Mars—specifically on the lower slopes of Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons) inside Gale Crater.

The system combines real historical data from NASA's Curiosity rover with a simulated tactical environment where a crew of astronauts departs from a central station toward three key scientific targets:

Gould Mesa: A stratigraphic overlook used to study sedimentary layers and Dark Ridges.

Mount Sharp: A geological unit rich in magnesium sulfates and calcium sulfate veins linked to ancient groundwater.

Ayopaya: A "Y"-shaped intersection of cemented ridges for photogrammetric surveying.

Real-Time Technical Operation:

Combinable and interactive hazard layers: Users can toggle Radiation, Thermal, and Topographic filters on or off, or tap directly anywhere on the orbital map to insert new hazards in real time as simulations.

Automatic geometric avoidance engine: Upon detecting an active hazard along a corridor, the algorithm instantly recalculates safe curved Outbound (solid line) and Return (dashed line) trajectories around the hazard perimeter with a constant safety buffer, avoiding blocking access nodes.

PLSS life-support telemetry: Models the real capacity of NASA's Primary Life Support System backpack, offering a nominal autonomy of 6.5 to 8 hours plus the Secondary Oxygen Pack (SOP:30 additional minutes for emergencies). Whenever a route detours around a hazard, the system recalculates the updated consumption in psi and alerts the astronaut to return to Base A for a refill without compromising the emergency SOP reserve.

A.R.E.S. AI tactical copilot: An integrated intelligent assistance module continuously monitors routes, explains which hazard triggered each detour, reports the exact increase in pressure consumed, and answers basic crew queries.

2. What benefits does it offer?

Crew safety: Prevents astronauts from crossing high-radiation zones, extreme cold pockets, or hazardous slopes through automatic detours calculated in milliseconds.

Oxygen management: Translates every additional meter of a detour into real pressure drop inside the PLSS backpack, preventing a seemingly short route from depleting the primary reserve and forcing the use of the secondary emergency pack.

Agile decision-making under contingencies: Enables step-by-step simulation of cumulative scenarios (such as solar storms or thermal shifts) and instantly evaluates which of the three routes remains viable.

Rigorous scientific traceability: Integrates tactical navigation on a single screen alongside real surface photographs (NASA/JPL Mastcam and Navcam cameras) and non-invasive sampling protocols.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Conceptual support for future crewed Mars missions: Serves as a functional interface prototype (HUD/wrist tablet or habitat console) for planning safe pedestrian traverses in hostile planetary environments.

Bridge between robotic and human exploration: Demonstrates how data gathered today by rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance form the direct foundation for designing future human expeditions in Gale Crater.

Transparent science education and outreach: Helps students, researchers, and the general public understand both Martian geology and the real limits of orbital sensors and spacesuits by explicitly separating real NASA data from simulated variables.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used?

Interface design and prototyping: Figma (primary design for the entire application).

Programming languages and frameworks: JavaScript with React for reactive state management and the trajectory calculation engine, and Tailwind CSS for responsive design.

Graphics and geospatial rendering: Interactive vector SVG (for dynamic routes, hazard polygons, contour lines, and tactical markers).

Libraries and development environment: Vite, Node.js, Lucide React (technical iconography), and Visual Studio Code.

Data sources and scientific reference software:

Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Mars Trek (https://trek.nasa.gov/mars/)

Curiosity Rover Route Map & Lower Mount Sharp (https://science.nasa.gov/mission/msl-curiosity/location-map/)

NASA Worldview / Earthdata (https://worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov/)

NASA Mars Raw Images Gallery — Mastcam and Navcam (https://mars.nasa.gov/mars2020/multimedia/raw-images/ and https://mars.nasa.gov/msl/multimedia/raw-images/)

5. How is your project creative?

Fusion of real robotic history with human planning: Instead of inventing a fictional map, we anchored the human stations directly onto three real landmarks investigated by Curiosity in 2025 (Gould Mesa, Mount Sharp, and Ayopaya), keeping their actual Mastcam and Navcam images as field guides for the astronauts.

Interactive map: Transforms a static map into a live tactical simulator where any user can challenge the AI by tapping the screen to generate radiation, extreme cold, or terrain zones and watch routes and oxygen consumption in$\text{psi}$adapt instantaneously.

Realistic life-support integration in navigation: Few prototypes link the geometry of a map detour directly to the physics of the PLSS spacesuit backpack and the operational rule of never encroaching on the 30 minute emergency SOP reserve.

"Honest Map" philosophy: The design features a dedicated section that transparently distinguishes which data come directly from NASA and which parameters are simulated for the engineering exercise.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Real EVA life-support engineering (NASA PLSS and SOP): Based on actual NASA spacesuit specifications: a primary backpack holding 0.54 kg of oxygen at approximately 7,500 psi, providing 6.5 to 8 hours of autonomy, plus a 30 minute Secondary Oxygen Pack (SOP) that must never be used for routine planning.

Surface physiology and operational timelines: Accounted for an average EVA walking speed of 0.45 m/s, 15 minutes of stationary scientific work at each stop, and a 30% safety reserve factor.

Martian environmental thresholds: Established clear operational limits to trigger detours: radiation exposure, cryogenic ground temperatures, and critical relative-elevation slopes.

Orbital sensor resolution and uncertainty: The team analyzed resolution limitations between orbital imagery and local surface sensors, incorporating perimeter safety buffers around each hazard polygon.

Scientific preservation of the environment: Included explicit protocols on the mission cards to prevent astronauts from stepping on or damaging fragile geological formations, such as the "Y"-shaped cemented ridges at Ayopaya.
